name: The Wybicki Oak

location.address: Park of the National Anthem Museum, Będomin, Kościerzyna County, Pomeranian Voivodeship, Poland

access: Paid entry to the National Anthem Museum grounds (branch of the National Museum in Gdansk): 7 zl normal / 3 zl reduced / 15 zl family, free on Fridays and Saturdays; open Tue-Sun, closed Mondays.
transport: Rural village roughly 10-15 km from Koscierzyna; PKS bus connections run from Koscierzyna, no railway station in Bedomin itself. Free parking at the museum.
verify_notes: Grows in the park of the 18th-century manor house where Jozef Wybicki, author of the words of the Polish national anthem (Mazurek Dabrowskiego), was born in 1747 and grew up; family tradition (repeated by the regional tourism board's own writeup) says the young Wybicki played beneath this oak. The manor is now the National Anthem Museum, a branch of the National Museum in Gdansk, open since 1978. Won Poland's national 'Tree of the Year 2013' competition (Klub Gaja) and placed 3rd in the European Tree of the Year 2014 with nearly 17,000 votes. Two independent sources plus a dedicated Polish tree database (bazadrzew.pl, which gives a precise coordinate matching the brief's estimate within about 15m) agree it is a pedunculate oak roughly 400 years old (one source says 440). Girth figures vary slightly across sources: 680cm (dzieje.pl/lasy.gov.pl coverage, pomorskie.travel), 673cm (bazadrzew.pl), 635cm (pl.wikipedia infobox); recorded 680cm as the most-repeated figure, note the spread for the writer. Height given once as 27m (2013 measurement), not independently corroborated. ALIVE: flagged rather than confirmed outright; newest dated evidence found is a 1 May 2019 article (nowepomorze.pl) reporting the tree still standing but weakened, with supports and cabling added to its heavy limbs against storm damage, and a genetic in-vitro clone planted alongside it the same year. No report of it having since died or fallen was found, and it is clearly still a live attraction (the museum's own current tourism copy continues to describe it as growing there). Worth-the-trip: this is a destination-test case, a single tree in a small museum's grounds with no other candidate nearby; it likely would not clear the single-famous-tree bar on the tree alone, but the combination of a national-anthem author's own boyhood tree plus a national tree-of-the-year title is a stronger case than most standalone candidates. Container decision left to whoever builds this place.

name: Helena the Poplar

location.address: Corner of ul. Baltycka, ul. Wiejska and ul. Kuracyjna, Hel, Puck County, Pomeranian Voivodeship, Poland

access: Free, on a public street corner in the middle of town.
transport: Central Hel, short walk from Hel railway station (the narrow-gauge line along the Hel Peninsula terminates in the town).
verify_notes: A black poplar (topola czarna) standing at the corner of Baltycka, Wiejska and Kuracyjna streets, most likely planted in the early 19th century, roughly 220 years old, height 30m, girth just over 4m (405cm per dzieje.pl, 'over 4 metres' per nadmorski24.pl). Designated a natural monument (pomnik przyrody) by the Gdansk Provincial National Council in 1973. Named Helena in 2017 when nominated for and won the national 'Tree of the Year' (Drzewo Roku) competition by Klub Gaja, after Helena Przybyszewska, wife of Commander Zbigniew Przybyszewski who commanded the 32-day defence of the Hel Peninsula in September 1939 (worth checking: sources differ slightly on exactly which Przybyszewski/spelling, writer should double check the commander's name before printing it as fact). Once stood beside a twin poplar that fell in a windstorm; the remaining trunk from that twin was carved into a sculpture of fishermen hauling nets, referencing Hel's fishing history, and stands near Helena today. ALIVE and thriving: described as the town's best-known tree, has its own Facebook page, and the town holds an annual 'name day' street celebration for it on 22 May, which is recent, ongoing, strong evidence of current life and of public access. Two independent sources agree on all core facts (age, species, girth, height, 1973 designation, 2017 naming). Location_precision confirmed: exact street-corner intersection named twice, matching the brief's coordinate. CLUSTER NOTE: stands about 0.5km from candidate 'Swiety Franciszek' (see next entry), the Franciscan monastery oak also in Hel -- worth flagging as a possible two-tree Hel walk if the oak also verifies, though two trees alone is short of the four-tree floor for a standalone Hel city page. Worth-the-trip: on its own this reads as a town landmark rather than a reason to travel to Hel specifically (people go to Hel for the peninsula and beach, not this tree), but it is a strong, well-loved, well-documented specimen that would be a genuine bonus stop for anyone in town, or the seed of a small Hel cluster alongside the oak.
